title: Prefix-drift guard's settled-history count is taken from the pre-normalization message list, so it disagrees with the shape it is compared against and can spuriously abort a task
evidence: The per-turn prefix-shape guard hashes NORMALIZED (post-replay) messages: line 372-378 sets shapeRequest.Messages = normalizer.StableRequestMessages(request) (which runs replayMessages -> repairToolMessageSequence), and line 387 NewWirePrefixShape(shapeRequest, ...) records shape.MessageCount = len(shapeRequest.Messages) and HistoryHash over the normalized history (prefixshape.go:65-80). But line 444 stores e.lastSentMessageCount = len(messages), where messages (line 367) is built.Messages — the PRE-normalization list. On the next turn that stale count is passed as settledCount into NewWirePrefixShape, which slices the normalized history by it: settledHistoryCount = max(0, min(len(history), settledCount-1)) (prefixshape.go:66). repairToolMessageSequence exists precisely because 'a resumed, compacted, or provider-rescued history lost one result' (provider.go:369-372); in exactly those cases it ADDS synthetic tool results (provider.go:399-407) or drops orphan tool messages, so len(shapeRequest.Messages) != len(messages). Windowing does not cause this (GroupUnits breaks only on user messages, so tool groups stay intact), but resume-after-an-interrupted-tool-call does.
failure_scenario: A task is interrupted (Esc / process kill / disconnect) after the assistant tool_calls message is persisted but before all its tool results are appended, leaving a dangling call in the saved history. On resume, turn 1 builds the request: built.Messages has M messages; the provider normalizer's repairToolMessageSequence appends the missing synthetic tool result(s), so the wire/shape has M' = M+1 messages. shape.MessageCount = M', but e.lastSentMessageCount is set to M. On the next comparison turn, CompareShape slices the normalized history to M-1 instead of the M'-1 the previous shape's HistoryHash actually covered, so previous.HistoryHash != current.SettledHash even though history grew purely append-only. Because this is an ordinary turn with no invalidation event for the seq, turnloop.go:399-401 returns the fatal error 'stable request prefix changed without an invalidation event: history' and aborts. Every subsequent task re-hits the same false positive (e.lastShape stays set, h.messages stays malformed), effectively bricking the resumed session until compaction rewrites the tail.
fix: Set e.lastSentMessageCount = shape.MessageCount (equivalently len(shapeRequest.Messages)) at turnloop.go:444, so the settledCount fed to next turn's NewWirePrefixShape matches the normalized message list the shape and wire actually used. This changes only the diagnostic count, never any bytes sent to the provider, so it is cache-safe.
why_it_matters: The guard whose entire job is to detect illegitimate prefix-cache invalidation instead manufactures a false one and aborts otherwise-valid work — precisely on the resume/compaction/rescue paths repairToolMessageSequence was written to survive. It undermines the cache-drift protection (Constitution III) and is a user-visible correctness/workflow failure (priority 1).

verdict.reasoning:
The code does exactly what the finding claims, and the failure is reachable on the production gateway path.

title: TruncateMiddle's '[N characters trimmed from the middle]' count omits the marker's own length, so it under-reports how much was cut
evidence: dropped := len(runes) - maxChars (line 113) is used in the marker text, but the actual number of source runes removed is len(runes) - (head + tail) = len(runes) - budget, where budget = maxChars - len(marker) (line 116). title: apply_patch invalidates the ENTIRE inspection ledger and supersedes reads of files it never touched
evidence: InvalidateFor takes the global-wipe branch whenever `path == "" || name == "apply_patch" || name == "run_shell" || strings.HasPrefix(name, "mcp__")` (inspection.go:215-222): it clears l.signatures and l.coverage entirely and returns EVERY covered read's CallID. edit_file/multi_edit/write_file (which carry a `path`) instead take the precise `invalidatePathLocked` branch. For run_shell/mcp the touched set is genuinely unknowable, but apply_patch's touched files are deterministic — a unified diff only modifies the files named in its ---/+++ headers, and the codebase already extracts them via contract.ToolTargetPaths -> PatchTargetFiles (tooltarget.go:87-101). In the main scope the returned CallIDs flow to e.history.MarkSuperseded (dispatch.go:160), and trimAgedMessages trims a superseded result even when it sits inside the keepFull most-recent window (history.go:241-244: `if !(isAged || isSuperseded) { continue }`).
failure_scenario: Main loop reads file B (large, still valid) at turn 5, then applies a one-file patch to file A at turn 6. InvalidateFor(apply_patch) wipes the whole ledger and returns B's read CallID; MarkSuperseded flags B. why_it_matters: Caching is the top project priority; this over-invalidation forces re-reads and trims valid recent context on every apply_patch, exactly the 'drop cache more aggressively than needed' failure the beat targets.

title: grep/glob/list_files dedup has no fingerprint staleness check; an external change serves a stale 'already ran' block
evidence: Duplicate() for non-read_file readonly tools returns a hit purely on `l.signatures[callSignature(call)]` + intact() (inspection.go:114-116), with no staleness gate. read_file, by contrast, first calls coverageStaleLocked(key) (inspection.go:123-128) which re-stats mtime+size and re-reads on change. failure_scenario: The agent runs `grep foo internal/` at turn 3 (recorded). title: Compaction summarizer's aux usage shares the requestSeq counter, orphaning a same-turn fold event's RequestSeq
evidence: appendUsageLocked stamps `record.Seq = e.requestSeq + 1` and then `e.requestSeq = record.Seq` (usage.go:144,153) for ALL streams including the compaction summarizer's recordAuxUsage (maintenance.go:82-86). title: Idle/lifetime stream timeout surfaces as context.Canceled, so it is never retried and is mislabeled "stopped." — defeating the documented recovery design
evidence: chatOnce implements BOTH the first-byte lifetime timeout (line 159 `lifetime := time.AfterFunc(cfg.RequestLifetime, cancel)`) and the rolling idle timeout (line 232 `idle := time.AfterFunc(cfg.IdleTimeout, cancel)`) by calling the SAME `cancel` from `ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(parent)` (line 157). When the idle timer fires mid-stream, the blocked `scanner.Scan()` unblocks and `scanner.Err()` returns a raw `context canceled` error, which chatOnce returns at line 273-275 with streamed=true. I confirmed this empirically: with an AfterFunc(cancel) firing during an httptest SSE body read, `scanner.Err()` == `context canceled`, `errors.Is(err, context.Canceled)`==true, and `parent.Err()`==nil. Back in Chat, both recovery gates are keyed on `isNetworkError(err)` (lines 113 and 126), and isNetworkError (line 628-630) returns false for anything that `errors.Is` context.Canceled — so the network-retry is skipped AND the once-only stream-retry is skipped. The turn loop's fallback also fails: turnloop.go:426 calls recoverableChatError -> gateway.Recoverable, and Recoverable returns false for any error whose string contains "context canceled" (friendly.go:69-75). Finally FriendlyRequestError(context.Canceled) renders "stopped." (friendly.go:22-24). This directly contradicts the design rationale in provider.go:62-73, which sets CLI idle (110s) BELOW the gateway's (120s) specifically so "the CLI — the side that can actually recover, via the stream retry in Chat below — is the one that times out first" and so the timeout becomes "a retried turn" rather than "an unrecoverable transport error." The stream-retry actually only fires for an active connection reset/EOF (TestDiedStreamIsRetriedOnce hijacks+closes, yielding a network error), never for the silent-stall timeout the ordering was built for.
failure_scenario: A long DeepSeek/MiniMax turn is generating through the gateway when the upstream connection wedges (half-open TCP / network partition), so no bytes and no `: keep-alive` comments arrive for 110s. The CLI idle timer fires and cancels the request context. chatOnce returns `context canceled` with streamed=true. Chat's stream-retry branch is skipped (isNetworkError==false), the turn loop's Recoverable==false, and the task aborts showing the user "stopped." — as if they pressed Ctrl-C — discarding every completed step of the turn, even though re-sending the byte-identical request against the still-warm cached prefix (a ~2s cache-priced retry) would have recovered it. Because the CLI cancels FIRST, it converts what would have been a retryable gateway-close EOF (at 120s) into a non-retryable cancellation.
fix: Distinguish a timeout-induced cancel from a user cancel. Track which fired (e.g. an atomic bool set in the AfterFunc before calling cancel, or separate cause tracking), and in chatOnce return a retryable timeout signal instead of raw context.Canceled when `parent.Err()==nil` — either wrap context.DeadlineExceeded (which isNetworkError already excludes but Recoverable(line 85) accepts) or a typed StalledError that Recoverable/isNetworkError treat as retryable. CACHE-SAFE: touches only error classification/timeout signaling; request bytes are unchanged and the retry re-sends the identical warm-prefix request.
why_it_matters: A recoverable transient stall aborts an entire multi-turn task and is reported to the user as a self-cancellation. The timeout ordering that was carefully designed to enable recovery instead guarantees non-recovery for exactly the stall case it targets.

title: Subagent turn-extension ladder's progress signal ignores apply_patch and run_shell writes, wrapping up productive executors early
evidence: The subagent ladder extends a run only while capture.touchedCount() grows (subagent.go:522-535: 'if touched := capture.touchedCount(); touched > progressMark ...'). touchedCount() is len(reads)+len(writes) from agentRunCapture.note (contextrecord.go:114-131), which records a path ONLY for read_file/edit_file/multi_edit/write_file. apply_patch (a registered workspace edit tool, registry.go:34, taking a 'patch' arg not 'path') and run_shell are deliberately excluded (contextrecord.go:109-113 — opaque). That opaqueness is harmless for the STALENESS use of touchedCount, but the SAME counter is reused as the ladder's PROGRESS signal (contextrecord.go:133-136), where an uncounted write is invisible work. general (the primary executor under the plan/execute split) has all tools and commonly edits via apply_patch.
failure_scenario: A 'general' continuation is dispatched to finish an implementation. capture is pre-seeded with the predecessor's touched paths (contextlink.go:323-330), so progressMark starts high. The executor now applies its changes with apply_patch on already-known files and verifies with run_shell (build/test) — neither increments touchedCount. At turn == turnCap (baseTurns), capture.touchedCount() == progressMark, so the ladder takes the else branch, sets wrapUp=true and forces the run to stop and report while it is actively landing edits. The run returns a partial (status labeled partial), and the parent must dispatch an unnecessary continuation to finish — extra cost and latency for work that was progressing.

In the subagent postDispatch (subagent.go:308-333), increment a dedicated progress counter for every successful mutation (isMutation(name) && !IsReadOnlyShell), or have agentRunCapture.note record apply_patch targets (parse the diff's +++ headers) and treat a successful non-read-only run_shell as a progress tick. Keep the staleness fingerprint set separate if opacity there is still wanted. Control-flow only; no prefix impact.
why_it_matters: Systematically biases the executor toward premature wrap-up, producing partial results and redundant continuation dispatches — the opposite of the ladder's stated intent (extend while real work lands).

verdict.reasoning:
The finding's factual core is grounded in the real code. touchedCount() (contextrecord.go:137-142) = len(reads)+len(writes), and note() (contextrecord.go:114-131) only records read_file/edit_file/multi_edit/write_file, unmarshaling solely a "path" field. apply_patch carries a "patch" arg not "path" (tooltarget.go:20-24) and run_shell has no path, so both are invisible to the counter. So a productive apply_patch-only executor CAN be wrapped up early — the defect is real.

It claims the run "returns a partial (status labeled partial), and the parent must dispatch an unnecessary continuation." A ladder wrap-up returns "done" with terminalShape wrapup-done, so the parent receives no partial signal and is not forced to dispatch a continuation. The finding also omits a compensating mechanism: at finalize, report-trailer Changed paths are folded into the write set (contextrecord.go:271-278), fixing the successor's RECORD (though too late for the live ladder decision).

Reachability is narrow: for general, baseTurns is 18-34 (MaxTurns 24 * AgentTurnScale .75-1.4, effort.go:37-58). The bug only bites if a continuation touches ZERO new counted paths across all those turns — a single new read_file or edit_file extends the ladder. Pure apply_patch+run_shell continuations on already-known files are plausible but not the common case, so "general commonly edits via apply_patch" overstates frequency. View()'s modal branch computes `available := max(4, m.height-lineCount(header)-lineCount(hint))` (view.go:36) and then `if len(rows) > available { rows = rows[:available] }` (view.go:49-50). renderHeader always returns 4 rows and renderModeLine returns 2 rows whenever the 'Shift + Tab to cycle' hint fits (it always fits above the 60-col floor, since the hint is ~20 cols and the gate is m.width-3), so available = m.height-6 — two rows fewer than renderModal assumed. A modal whose content fills its budget is thus clamped by 2 rows from the bottom.
failure_scenario: A many-choice /resume or /skills modal (or a full /context) that fills its height on a 24-30 row terminal renders without its bottom border (pad row + bottom border are the two rows dropped, since pad=1 at all above-floor heights). fix: Compute renderModal's budget from the same quantity View() reserves (`m.height - lineCount(header) - lineCount(modeLine)`), or have View() pass that budget in, so the two agree. Cache-safe: presentation-only.

title: Grep/List/Glob read protected credential roots by targeting a non-sensitive ancestor
evidence: ApprovePath denies any target that IsInside a sensitive root (permissions.go:103-108; roots = ~/.muhiya, ~/.ssh, ~/.gnupg, ~/.aws, ~/.azure, ~/.kube per paths.go:120-137). But the directory-traversing tools authorize only the single root path once: Grep/List/Glob call authorizePath->ApprovePath exactly once (files.go:361 is the only ApprovePath call in the file; grep confirmed via grep -n). They then enumerate children via collectFiles (files.go:148) + readTextFile (files.go:167) for Grep, WalkDir (files.go:46) for List, and WalkDir (files.go:196) for Glob, with NO per-file sensitive-root check. ActionRead/ActionSearch are non-mutating (types.go:47-48), and the outside-workspace confirm in ApprovePath (permissions.go:109-124) fires for the ancestor, not for the credential files under it. WalkDir does not descend symlinks and collectFiles skips non-regular entries, so the leak is specifically a real ancestor directory (home, drive root) that is not itself a sensitive root.
failure_scenario: Model (or prompt-injected instruction) calls grep{path:"~", pattern:"PRIVATE KEY"} or grep{path:"~", pattern:"."}. ~ is not a sensitive root, so ApprovePath issues only a single 'search wants access outside the workspace' confirm naming the home dir; the user approves searching home. Grep then reads ~/.ssh/id_rsa, ~/.aws/credentials, ~/.muhiya/secrets.json contents and returns matching lines into the model context and the (nested-token-blind) transcript. Direct grep{path:"~/.ssh"} IS blocked, but its non-sensitive ancestor is not — directly violating docs/security.md line 8: credential roots 'are denied even when the user would otherwise approve outside access.'
fix: Enforce sensitive-root denial on every path the search tools TRAVERSE, not just the authorized root. Thread the guard's g.sensitive list (or a Workspace.isSensitive helper) into collectFiles, the Grep read loop, and the List/Glob WalkDir callbacks: SkipDir when a directory IsInside a sensitive root and skip any file whose path IsInside one. Runtime-only change, no prompt/schema bytes touched — cache-safe.
why_it_matters: Leaks SSH private keys, AWS credentials, and MuhiyaCode's own secrets into model context/transcript, defeating the single strongest documented containment guarantee.

verdict.reasoning:
The mechanism is real and reachable. ApprovePath (permissions.go:98-108) denies a target ONLY when `IsInside(sensitiveRoot, canonical)` is true — i.e. only when the target is a sensitive root or a descendant of one. A non-sensitive ANCESTOR (the home dir, a drive root) that CONTAINS the credential roots passes this check: IsInside(~/.ssh, ~) is false because ~ is the parent, not a child. authorizePath (files.go:356-362) calls ApprovePath exactly once on the single root target; grep confirms this is the only ApprovePath call in files.go. The directory-traversing tools then enumerate children with NO per-file sensitive check: Grep -> collectFiles (files.go:494-516, only skips ignoredNames = .git/node_modules/vendor/etc., NOT .ssh/.aws/.muhiya) then readTextFile on each (files.go:167); List -> WalkDir (files.go:46-76); Glob -> WalkDir (files.go:196-222). ActionRead/ActionSearch are non-mutating (types.go:47-48 Mutates() returns false for read/search), so the only gate that fires is the single outside-workspace confirm (permissions.go:109-124), which names the ancestor dir, not the credential files beneath it. This defeats the guarantee documented verbatim at docs/security.md line 8: credential roots "are denied even when the user would otherwise approve outside access." The shell path IS defended (sensitiveShellReference textual backstop, permissions.go:182-189) and GitDiff has a test (workspace_test.go:310), but Grep/List/Glob traversal has no equivalent per-entry guard.

One correction to the reporter's example: Resolve (paths.go:82-90) does NOT expand `~` — there is no tilde expansion anywhere (grep for UserHomeDir/expandTilde shows only defaultSensitiveRoots and skills use it). So a literal `grep{path:"~"}` resolves to a bogus `<workspace>/~` dir inside the workspace and would not reach home. This is only a notational flaw in the PoC, not a refutation: the reporter explicitly names "home, drive root" as the ancestor, and the exploit is trivially reachable with an absolute path — grep{path:"C:\\Users\\mydwa", pattern:"PRIVATE KEY"} or grep{path:"C:\\"} (or /home/user on POSIX). Home is not a sensitive root, so ApprovePath issues a single outside-workspace confirm, and on approval collectFiles walks into ~/.ssh/id_rsa, ~/.aws/credentials, ~/.muhiya/* and readTextFile returns their contents into model context and transcript. Reachable and correct as described.
verdict.fix_assessment: Correct and cache-safe. Threading the guard's g.sensitive list into collectFiles, the Grep read loop, and the List/Glob WalkDir callbacks (SkipDir when a dir IsInside a sensitive root, skip any file IsInside one) is a runtime-only enforcement change. It touches no system prompt, tool schema, or wire bytes, so it cannot perturb the byte-stable cached prefix (Constitution III/IV preserved). It strengthens rather than breaks existing tests: workspace_test.go asserts direct sensitive-root targeting is blocked (unaffected) and GitDiff blocking (unaffected); adding per-entry skipping is pure defense-in-depth. Minor implementation note: collectFiles is a free function today, so the guard's sensitive set (or a Workspace.isSensitive helper wrapping g.sensitive + IsInside) must be threaded in — straightforward and does not alter any cached surface.
verdict.cache_regression_risk: None. The fix is confined to filesystem-traversal enforcement in internal/workspace (runtime path). It emits no prompt/schema/history bytes and changes no request params, so the deterministic cached prefix is untouched; degrades gracefully across providers since it is provider-independent.

title: MCP OAuth access/refresh tokens and client_secret are never added to the exact-match redaction set
evidence: mcpSecretValues builds the exact-secret list by collecting only TOP-LEVEL string values from each secrets.OAuth[name] map (root.go:538-544: `for _,value:=range server { if text,ok:=value.(string) ...}`). But the actual bearer secrets live NESTED: entry["tokens"] is a map{access_token,refresh_token,...} (auth.go:119 via encodeOAuthToken tokens.go:109-118) and client_secret lives under entry["clientInformation"] (map, tokens.go:74-80). Being maps, they are skipped, so access_token/refresh_token/client_secret never enter the exact-match set. state.Redact then only exact-matches the values it is given plus three generic regexes (session.go:323-340). Worse, transcript persistence passes NO extra values at all (session.go:61 calls redactObject->Redact with no extra), so MCP secrets get only generic-pattern coverage there. Meanwhile the harmless URL fields (tokenEndpoint/resourceUrl) ARE added as 'secrets'.
failure_scenario: User authorizes an OAuth MCP server; stored token is an opaque bare string (e.g. 'ya29.a0Af...') that is not in Bearer/sk-/access_token= shape. An MCP tool result echoes it, or the model paraphrases it into a save_memory candidate or a harness-event detail. e.redact (state.Redact with secretValues[1:]) does not contain the token (it was nested), and no generic pattern matches a bare opaque token, so it is written verbatim into the memory file, harness event, and events DB — contradicting docs/security.md 'Transcripts/events redact configured exact secrets'.
fix: In mcpSecretValues, recurse into nested maps/slices and collect every string leaf >=8 chars (covers tokens.access_token/refresh_token and clientInformation.client_secret). Also pass the full MCP secret set into transcript redaction (Sessions.Secrets currently only carries ProviderAPIKey). Cache-safe (redaction is off-prefix).
why_it_matters: The exact-secret redaction promised for MCP secrets structurally excludes the very tokens it is meant to protect, leaving defense-in-depth to generic regexes that miss bare tokens.

verdict.reasoning: Verified directly in the real files (the finding's cited paths were slightly off — actual files are internal/command/root.go, internal/mcpclient/tokens.go & auth.go, internal/state/session.go). mcpSecretValues (root.go:537-544) iterates the OAuth[name] map and appends only values passing value.(string); the actual bearer secrets live in nested maps — entry["tokens"] (access_token/refresh_token, encodeOAuthToken tokens.go:109-118) and entry["clientInformation"] (client_secret, oauthClient tokens.go:74-80). Those maps fail the string assertion and are dropped. Confirmed the only top-level STRINGS stored are the harmless URLs tokenEndpoint/authorizationServerUrl/resourceUrl (auth.go:127-133), so the exact-match set inverts as claimed: URLs in, tokens out. Engine redact is wired with secretValues[1:] (runtime_build.go:562), which is exactly this token-less MCP set, feeding all e.redact call sites (memory save_memory, telemetry, harness events, tool targets). Transcript persistence (session.go:61) calls redactObject->Redact with s.Secrets and no extra values, so MCP tokens get only ProviderAPIKey exact-match plus the three generic regexes. Confirmed the generic patterns (session.go:323-327) only fire on sk-/Bearer prefixes or key[:=]value shape — a bare opaque token (ya29.a0Af...) echoed alone matches none. The promised exact-match redaction for MCP secrets is therefore structurally defeated for the real tokens. Reachability of the worst case is real but moderate: OAuth tokens normally travel in Authorization headers, not tool results, so a verbatim echo into a transcript/memory is uncommon though non-zero (introspection/echo tools, model paraphrase). The structural gap itself is unconditional.
verdict.fix_assessment: Correct. Recursing into nested maps/slices and collecting string leaves >=8 chars captures access_token, refresh_token, and client_secret; it also incidentally collects the expiry timestamp and the URLs (already collected), a cosmetic over-redaction, not a functional regression. Passing the full MCP secret set into transcript redaction (session.go redactObject path) closes the second gap. Both changes are correct and address the root cause.
verdict.cache_regression_risk: None. Redaction operates entirely off the cached prefix — it rewrites memory-file content, transcript JSONL, and harness/event detail strings, never the system prompt, tool schemas, or settled history. No golden prefix test (prefix_bytes.golden, prefix_bytes_wire.golden) covers redacted output, and no provider wire shape depends on it. Cache-safe.

title: PowerShell delete aliases with abbreviated -r/-fo switches bypass the recursive-force-delete block
evidence: The alias guard hard-requires the LITERAL substrings '-recurse' AND '-force' (risk.go:91: `(Contains(lower,"remove-item") || recursiveDeleteAlias.Match) && Contains(lower,"-recurse") && Contains(lower,"-force")`). Only 'remove-item' gets the abbreviation-tolerant regex shellRiskPatterns[0] (risk.go:19, `-(?:[a-z]*r[a-z]*|recurse)...-(?:[a-z]*f[a-z]*|force)`). The aliases ri/del/erase/rd/rmdir (recursiveDeleteAlias, risk.go:42) are all Remove-Item aliases that accept abbreviated switches -r/-rec and -fo/-for, which the literal Contains-check misses. The cmd-oriented patterns[1]/[2] only catch '/s' '/q'. So `ri -r -fo <path>` matches the alias branch but fails the '-recurse'/'-force' Contains, matches no shellRiskPattern, and is not caught by rmCommand (which needs literal `rm`).
failure_scenario: Model runs `ri -r -fo C:\Users\me\Documents` or `rd -r -fo /` (valid PowerShell: -r->Recurse, -fo->Force, both unambiguous). ClassifyShell returns not-blocked. In auto-accept mode on a trusted workspace, ApproveShell returns nil with zero confirmation (permissions.go:157-160), so the recursive force delete executes — bypassing the 'recursive-force deletion ... blocked ... fail-closed' guarantee (docs/security.md:10,13).
fix: Apply the same abbreviation-tolerant recurse/force detection to the alias forms as remove-item gets: after matching an alias, test for any `-r*` switch AND any `-f*` switch (e.g. reuse the `[a-z]*r[a-z]*` / `[a-z]*f[a-z]*` shape), instead of Contains('-recurse')&&Contains('-force'). Cache-safe.
why_it_matters: A trivially reachable spelling of a catastrophic delete is unblocked and, in auto-accept, runs unconfirmed.

verdict.reasoning: Opened risk.go. Line 91's alias branch requires the LITERAL substrings `-recurse` AND `-force` via strings.Contains: `(Contains(lower,"remove-item") || recursiveDeleteAlias.Match) && Contains(lower,"-recurse") && Contains(lower,"-force")`. The abbreviation-tolerant regex (shellRiskPatterns[0], line 19) fires only on literal `remove-item`, not aliases. The cmd-style del/erase (line 20) and rmdir/rd (line 21) patterns require `/s` or `/q`. rmCommand (line 64) requires literal `rm`. recursiveDeleteAlias (line 42) matches ri/del/erase/rd/rmdir. Traced `ri -r -fo C:\path`: alias regex matches, but Contains("-recurse") is false (only `-r`), so line-91 condition is false; no shellRiskPattern matches; rmCommand needs `rm`; result is ShellRisk{} (not blocked). PowerShell validity holds: ri/del/erase/rd/rmdir are Remove-Item aliases; `-r`→-Recurse and `-fo`→-Force are both unambiguous (the finding correctly avoided the ambiguous `-f`). Reachability to unconfirmed execution confirmed at permissions.go:147-161: ApproveShell calls ClassifyShell; when not blocked and Mode()==PermissionAutoAccept it returns nil with no confirmation. So on a trusted workspace in auto-accept, `ri -r -fo <path>` / `rd -r -fo /` runs the recursive force delete silently, defeating the documented fail-closed guarantee.

Applying the same `[a-z]*r[a-z]*` / `[a-z]*f[a-z]*` abbreviation-tolerant recurse/force detection to alias forms closes the gap. risk.go is runtime shell classification, not part of the byte-stable prompt prefix or tool schemas, so the change touches no golden files and no provider prefix. title: read_skill returns file contents through a symlinked SKILL.md, bypassing sensitive-root containment
evidence: read_skill is correctly name-keyed (skills_tool.go:126-154): the model supplies only a name, resolved against the frozen catalog, and loadSkill reads entry.Path — it cannot be steered at an arbitrary path, as documented. HOWEVER entry.Path is whatever SKILL.md discovery found, and LoadSkillInstructions just os.Open(skill.Path) + LimitReader (skills.go:25-30) with NO EvalSymlinks and NO sensitive-root check. DiscoverSkills likewise follows the file when reading frontmatter (skills.go:117-121). So a SKILL.md that is a symlink to an arbitrary file is cataloged (name falls back to parent-dir basename when the target has no frontmatter, skills.go:144-147) and its target's first 32 KiB is returned as tool output. This reaches files the file tools would block (~/.ssh/id_rsa), so the doc's 'cannot be steered at an arbitrary file' is not strictly true for file CONTENTS.
failure_scenario: An attacker (or malicious skill package) with write access to any skill root — e.g. ~/.agents/skills — creates ~/.agents/skills/x/SKILL.md as a symlink to ~/.ssh/id_rsa. At next session it is discovered and advertised; the model calls read_skill{name:"x"} and receives the private key, even though read_file ~/.ssh/id_rsa is hard-blocked by ApprovePath. Precondition (local write to a trusted skill dir) is high, which is why this is low, but it is a genuine escalation from 'influence instructions' to 'exfiltrate arbitrary file contents' and sharpens the docs' overclaim.
fix: Before reading, EvalSymlinks(skill.Path) and reject (or skip at discovery) any SKILL.md whose real path resolves inside a sensitive root; optionally reject SKILL.md files that are symlinks entirely. Cache-safe (does not alter the advertised catalog bytes for legitimate skills).
why_it_matters: Provides a second tool path that reads credential files the file-tool containment is designed to deny.

verdict.reasoning: low/polish severity — passed through without adversarial verification

evidence: ContextReport.HistoryTokens = e.history.EstimatedTokens() (contextreport.go:56) and ContextReport.Percent = float64(history)/limit*100 (contextreport.go:77). estimatedLocked() sums ONLY the compact summary + the message log (history.go:579-588); the system prompt and tool schemas are deliberately NOT in the message log (Calibrate comment, history.go:616-617: "the system prompt is not stored in the message log but IS counted in promptTokens"). title: read_skill's provided-set resets every task, so re-reading a skill later in the same session re-sends a body already in settled history
evidence: taskSkillsProvided is cleared each task in resetTaskState (engine.go:376) and then seeded ONLY from the current prompt's manual <skill name="..."> markers via seedProvidedSkills (skills_tool.go:177-182). skillAlreadyProvided/markSkillProvided (skills_tool.go:159-172) therefore track provision within one task only. readSkillTool re-loads and returns the full body whenever the name is not in this task's provided-set (skills_tool.go:142-153), and that body is appended to settled history as a RoleTool result (turnloop.go:574). Nothing seeds the provided-set from prior read_skill tool results already present in the append-only history.
failure_scenario: Session with two tasks on similar work. Task 1: model calls read_skill("frontend-design"); the full body enters history as a tool result and settles. Task 2 (same session): taskSkillsProvided starts empty (task-2 prompt has no manual skill marker), so read_skill("frontend-design") re-loads and re-sends the entire body — a second full copy of content already in context. It rides the append-only tail so the prefix is not invalidated, but it is redundant retransmission of settled content (Constitution V) that consumes uncached tail tokens on that turn.

The read_skill "already provided" path then also covers cross-task repeats. Tail-only change; prefix untouched.
why_it_matters: Caching is the top priority; this is a small but real Constitution V leak the harness could suppress.
